description: Goudiss, C. Houston and Alberta M. Goudiss. Foods that will Win the War and How to Cook Them . New York: Forecast, 1918. Contextual Background Published during the final year of World War I, Foods That Will Win the War and How to Cook Them was a direct response to the wartime food conservation campaign led by the United States Food Administration under Herbert Hoover. With Allied troops fighting on multiple fronts and agricultural output in Europe devastated, the burden of food supply fell heavily on the United States. The U.S. government mobilized civilians on the home front to conserve wheat, meat, sugar, and fats so that more could be exported to soldiers and civilians overseas. The Goudisses—a food expert and a domestic science educator—wrote this book to provide practical support for that campaign. The work is not merely a cookbook but a tool of civic and patriotic education. It exemplifies Progressive Era values of scientific management, home economics, and collective national effort. Recipes were designed to align with federal guidelines, such as wheatless and meatless days, and were tested under the supervision of domestic science experts. The text contains charts, substitution strategies, and detailed cooking instructions, emphasizing thrift, nutrition, and practicality. The underlying message is clear: everyday homemakers—particularly women—could wield profound influence over the war effort by modifying their cooking and eating habits. The slogan “Food will win the war” encapsulated this ethos, and the book served as both instructional manual and wartime propaganda. Thematic Summary 1. Total War and the Home Front The text exemplifies the concept of total war , where civilian populations are mobilized for military aims. Housewives are enlisted as frontline participants in the economic and logistical struggle of World War I, echoing the shift from battlefield-only engagements to wars involving whole societies. Food rationing and substitution become patriotic duties, connecting domestic labor to national victory. 2. Government and Civilian Cooperation Through its alignment with the U.S. Food Administration’s guidelines, the book illustrates a voluntary but heavily promoted form of government intervention . Rather than imposing strict rationing (as in Europe), the United States promoted conservation through education, propaganda, and civic duty. The work reveals the effectiveness of non-coercive state policy in democracies during wartime, and the role of media and experts in shaping compliance. 3. Scientific Management and Progressive Reform The Goudisses' approach to cooking and consumption is rooted in Progressive Era ideals —particularly home economics, efficiency, and rational consumption. The book instructs families to calculate calories, use substitutions, avoid waste, and follow tested recipes. This reflects the broader trend of applying scientific methods to domestic and social life during the early 20th century. 4. Gender, Domesticity, and National Identity The text assigns a pivotal wartime role to women, not in factories but in kitchens. It valorizes domestic labor and situates the housewife as a moral and economic agent in the war effort. This highlights how traditional gender roles were both challenged and reaffirmed in wartime, and invites discussion of how femininity was constructed in patriotic terms. 5. Propaganda, Morality, and Sacrifice Embedded within the recipes is a moral message: sacrifice in the kitchen supports soldiers at the front. Phrases like “every crumb counts” and statistics about waste evoke guilt and pride. This emotional appeal shows how propaganda was tailored to domestic spaces , forging a moral economy that equated thrift with heroism.   Relevant IB Global Politics Links: ·        Power and Sovereignty : Voluntary compliance to state directives. ·        Development : Food distribution, equity, and the moral economy in wartime. Relevant AP U.S. History Themes: ·        American and National Identity (NAT) : Gender roles and civic identity. ·        Work, Exchange, and Technology (WXT) : Wartime economics, food science. ·        Politics and Power (POL) : Role of the Food Administration. ·        Culture and Society (CUL) : Patriotism and propaganda on the home front. Description Foods That Will Win the War and How to Cook Them (1918) by C. Houston Goudiss and Alberta M. Goudiss is a wartime domestic science manual that blends patriotic instruction with practical guidance on food conservation during World War I. Produced in coordination with the U.S. Food Administration, the text addresses how American households—particularly women—could support the Allied war effort by modifying their cooking habits to save wheat, meat, sugar, and fats. It includes over 200 recipes, substitution strategies, nutritional charts, and tips for using leftovers, all aimed at maximizing efficiency and minimizing waste. The book is both a propaganda tool and a domestic guide, reflecting broader themes of total war, national unity, and Progressive Era ideals of scientific management in the home. It illustrates how domestic labor, consumer choices, and gendered civic duty became crucial components of wartime strategy. OPCVL Foods That Will Win the War and How to Cook Them (1918) is a valuable source for historians and political scientists studying U.S. domestic policy and civilian mobilization during World War I. Its origin—authored by food expert C. Houston Goudiss and domestic educator Alberta M. Goudiss in partnership with the U.S. Food Administration—places it at the intersection of public policy, propaganda, and Progressive Era reform. The purpose of the text was to persuade American households, especially women, to voluntarily adopt food conservation practices—such as substituting wheat, meat, sugar, and fats—to support the war effort. Through detailed recipes, nutritional charts, and substitution techniques, the book operationalizes wartime food policy into manageable household action, offering direct insight into how the U.S. government sought to influence behavior without formal rationing laws. However, the source has limitations. Its promotional and prescriptive tone reveals more about the idealized image of the patriotic homemaker than the actual success or failure of these policies on a national scale. It does not provide data on civilian resistance, regional disparities, or the socioeconomic burdens these policies may have imposed on working-class or immigrant households. The text also lacks voices from outside the white, middle-class, female demographic it was targeting. As a result, while it is a rich example of state-sanctioned propaganda and voluntary civic mobilization, it must be supplemented with quantitative data, oral histories, or critiques from contemporaneous sources to form a comprehensive picture of domestic wartime food policy and its impact. Lenses Foods That Will Win the War and How to Cook Them is deeply rooted in both Progressive-era civic republicanism and total war historical theory , with notable alignment to voluntarist models of governance and gendered civic duty frameworks. From a historical theory perspective, the text reflects the “total war” model , wherein civilian populations are mobilized in direct support of military objectives. This is evident in the authors’ assertion that domestic food choices are militarily consequential—“food will win the war.” The book treats the home front as an essential extension of the battlefield, integrating everyday behaviors like cooking and conserving into the broader war strategy. Additionally, it aligns with Progressive-era ideology , emphasizing scientific management, efficiency, and public education to solve national problems through rational planning and moral responsibility. From a civic duty lens , the text embodies a form of republican civic virtue , where individual sacrifice and participation in the collective good are considered hallmarks of citizenship. The domestic labor of women is framed as a patriotic contribution equal in value to that of soldiers, reifying a gendered vision of civic responsibility . The voluntarist tone—urging substitution rather than enforcing rationing—reflects liberal democratic values , where public compliance is assumed to arise from shared moral obligation rather than coercion. Thus, the work promotes a moral economy of sacrifice , where thrift and food conservation become instruments of national unity and democratic participation. OPCVL

Foods That Will Win the War and How to Cook Them (1918) is a valuable source for historians and political scientists studying U.S. domestic policy and civilian mobilization during World War I. Its origin—authored by food expert C. Houston Goudiss and domestic educator Alberta M. Goudiss in partnership with the U.S. Food Administration—places it at the intersection of public policy, propaganda, and Progressive Era reform. The purpose of the text was to persuade American households, especially women, to voluntarily adopt food conservation practices—such as substituting wheat, meat, sugar, and fats—to support the war effort. Through detailed recipes, nutritional charts, and substitution techniques, the book operationalizes wartime food policy into manageable household action, offering direct insight into how the U.S. government sought to influence behavior without formal rationing laws.

However, the source has limitations. Its promotional and prescriptive tone reveals more about the idealized image of the patriotic homemaker than the actual success or failure of these policies on a national scale. It does not provide data on civilian resistance, regional disparities, or the socioeconomic burdens these policies may have imposed on working-class or immigrant households. As a result, while it is a rich example of state-sanctioned propaganda and voluntary civic mobilization, it must be supplemented with quantitative data, oral histories, or critiques from contemporaneous sources to form a comprehensive picture of domestic wartime food policy and its impact.

Lenses

Foods That Will Win the War and How to Cook Them is deeply rooted in both Progressive-era civic republicanism and total war historical theory, with notable alignment to voluntarist models of governance and gendered civic duty frameworks.

From a historical theory perspective, the text reflects the “total war” model, wherein civilian populations are mobilized in direct support of military objectives. This is evident in the authors’ assertion that domestic food choices are militarily consequential—“food will win the war.” The book treats the home front as an essential extension of the battlefield, integrating everyday behaviors like cooking and conserving into the broader war strategy. Additionally, it aligns with Progressive-era ideology, emphasizing scientific management, efficiency, and public education to solve national problems through rational planning and moral responsibility.

From a civic duty lens, the text embodies a form of republican civic virtue, where individual sacrifice and participation in the collective good are considered hallmarks of citizenship. The domestic labor of women is framed as a patriotic contribution equal in value to that of soldiers, reifying a gendered vision of civic responsibility. The voluntarist tone—urging substitution rather than enforcing rationing—reflects liberal democratic values, where public compliance is assumed to arise from shared moral obligation rather than coercion. Thus, the work promotes a moral economy of sacrifice, where thrift and food conservation become instruments of national unity and democratic participation.

  • The redefinition of civic participation beyond military service.

Key Excerpts + Annotations (with Vocabulary Support)

“All it asks is that we substitute as far as possible corn and other cereals for wheat, reduce a little our meat consumption and save sugar and fats...”
Annotation: Highlights voluntary compliance and subtle state pressure.
Vocabulary: Substitute = replace; Consumption = use of food/resources.

“A little bit of saving in food means a tremendous aggregate total, when 100,000,000 people are doing the saving.”
Annotation: Shows collectivist moral logic—individual acts add up nationally.
Vocabulary: Aggregate = total; Saving = conservation.

“Even the baker’s rye loaf is usually made of one-half rye and one-half wheat.”
Annotation: Demonstrates scientific rationale behind food policy.
Vocabulary: Loaf = bread portion; Proportion = part relative to a whole.

“The woman in the home… must acquire those saving habits… if we are to secure a permanent peace.”
Annotation: Gendered framing of civic virtue and postwar future.
Vocabulary: Acquire = learn; Permanent = lasting; Civic virtue = duty to the republic.
